questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment to test biomagnification
questions.stem: Design an experiment to test whether a pollutant biomagnifies up a food chain.

answer.exemplar: Measure pollutant concentration in organisms at each trophic level of a controlled aquatic food chain and compare levels across levels.

questions.explanation: Comparing concentrations across trophic levels in a controlled chain tests magnification.
questions.hint: Measure toxin at each trophic level.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a biodiversity index from data
questions.stem: Two sites have the same species richness, but Site X has a higher Shannon index. What does this imply?

options.text: There is no difference between the sites.
Site X has more total individuals.
Site X has fewer species.
Site X has more even abundances across species.

questions.explanation: With equal richness, a higher Shannon index means more even distribution of individuals among species.
questions.hint: What does Shannon index reward besides richness?

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an energy pyramid from data
questions.stem: An energy pyramid shows 10000 kJ at producers and 100 kJ at secondary consumers. Is this consistent with the ten percent rule?

options.text: No, because energy should increase upward.
No, because it should be 1000 kJ.
options.misconception: applies one transfer instead of two

options.text: Yes, because two transfers of ten percent give 100 kJ.
Yes, because all energy is transferred.

questions.explanation: Two ten-percent transfers: 10000 to 1000 to 100 kJ, which matches. The data are consistent.
questions.hint: Apply ten percent twice.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an interaction matrix from data
questions.stem: A matrix shows Species A benefits and Species B is unaffected when they co-occur. What interaction is this?

options.text: Mutualism, because both are present.
Competition, because they share space.
Commensalism, because one benefits and the other is unaffected.
Parasitism, because one depends on the other.

questions.explanation: One benefits and the other is unaffected, which is commensalism.
questions.hint: Check the effect on each species.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a niche overlap graph
questions.stem: A graph shows two species with overlapping but not identical resource use curves. What does this suggest?

options.text: They cannot coexist and one will exclude the other.
options.misconception: overstates the consequence of partial overlap

options.text: No interaction occurs between them.
They have identical niches.
Partial overlap allows coexistence through resource partitioning.

questions.explanation: Partial overlap means some competition, but partitioning can allow coexistence.
questions.hint: Does partial overlap imply total exclusion?

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a catch-per-unit-effort trend
questions.stem: Catch per unit effort (CPUE) declines steadily over a decade. What does this indicate?

options.text: The stock is increasing.
options.misconception: confuses declining CPUE with stock growth

options.text: Fishing is becoming more efficient.
options.misconception: reverses the meaning of declining CPUE

options.text: The stock is likely declining.
Effort has no effect on catch.

questions.explanation: Declining CPUE means more effort is needed per unit catch, signalling a declining stock.
questions.hint: What does falling catch per effort imply?
